records.citation: Smith SJ, Wiberg K, McCleaf P, Ahrens L. Pilot-Scale Continuous Foam Fractionation for the Removal of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from Landfill Leachate. ACS ES&T Water. 2022;2:841–851.

comparability.reason: Study reports PFAS removal percentages for a pilot-scale continuous foam fractionation system treating a defined landfill leachate matrix, with clear distinction between sum PFAS, long-chain, and short-chain species and explicit identification of operation modes, allowing conditional comparison with other foam fractionation studies under similar matrices and scales.

endpoints.interpretation: Sum PFAS removal in the continuous pilot column plateaued at about 60%. Individual long-chain PFAS were removed by more than 90%, whereas select short-chain PFAS showed low removals below about 30%. These are phase-transfer removals to foam, not degradation.

Authors concluded that differences in treatment efficiency between enriching vs stripping modes and between continuous vs batch operation were negligible, and that continuous foam fractionation is a highly applicable technology for PFAS-contaminated water.

limitations.statement: Evidence is based on a single natural landfill leachate matrix treated in a pilot-scale system, which may limit generalizability to other waters and scales.

Continuous vs batch and enriching vs stripping modes showed negligible differences in treatment efficiency under the tested conditions, so findings on mode-dependent performance are constrained to the specific operating regime studied.

operating_conditions.value: continuous and batch foam fractionation compared; enriching vs stripping modes in continuous column

pfas_scope.value: sum PFAS (aggregate of measured PFAS species)

quantitative_findings.name: sum PFAS removal efficiency (continuous pilot column, plateau)
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: plateaued at about 60% removal in continuous pilot foam fractionation of landfill leachate

residuals_byproducts.statement: Authors recommend that the PFAS-enriched foamate be coupled to an energy-intensive degradative technology for concentrated foam destruction as part of an on-site remediation train; this downstream treatment was proposed but not experimentally evaluated in the study.

Improved foam collection (e.g., vacuum-assisted collection) and arranging multiple foam fractionation steps in series were suggested to boost short-chain PFAS removal and overall performance, indicating that short-chain PFAS may remain in the treated effluent under the reported single-pass conditions.

comparability.reason: The study reports PFAS percentage removal from landfill leachate using a defined ozone foam fractionation configuration (specified gas flow, ozone dose, and minimized foamate volume) and focuses on long-chain PFAS; these metrics can be compared with other foam fractionation or concentration steps treating similar landfill leachate matrices and reporting percent removal of comparable PFAS classes, but may not be directly comparable to studies on different matrices or with different endpoints (e.g., destruction or mineralization).

Downstream treatment or disposal options for the PFAS-enriched ozonated foamate are not experimentally evaluated; the work characterizes the concentration step only.
Energy consumption of ozone generation and overall process is not fully quantified in the available description.

Key operational details such as feed and foamate volumes, operating duration, and enrichment factors are not explicitly reported in the provided excerpts, limiting assessment of scalability and mass balance.

records.citation: Newman P. Converting PFAS-Impacted Landfill Leachate Waste from a Liquid to a Solid: Using Full-Scale Foam Fractionation and Media Superloading to Minimize Waste and Reduce Risk. ESAA Remediation Technologies Symposium abstract. 2026.

comparability.reason: The abstract provides qualitative description of a full-scale landfill leachate foam fractionation and Superloading system, with limited quantitative information (goals and approximate concentration factors) and no PFAS speciation, influent concentrations, or detailed operational parameters; this restricts direct quantitative comparison with other foam fractionation studies and treatment trains.

endpoints.interpretation: Treatment goal is 75% removal of PFAS mass from landfill leachate; the abstract does not clearly state whether this value is achieved or targeted, so it is treated as a design/operational goal rather than a confirmed performance metric.

System performance includes concentrating PFAS from bulk leachate into smaller-volume waste streams: Superloading media treatment of foamate yields up to an additional 500-fold concentration of PFAS into solid media, giving an overall landfill PFAS waste concentration factor of approximately 1000–2000-fold relative to the original liquid leachate. This reflects phase transfer and enrichment, not chemical degradation.
Design objective that short-chain PFAS should constitute less than about 45% of total PFAS mass; the abstract does not report achieved values or specific short-chain species behavior.

limitations.statement: Information is drawn from a one-page conference abstract, so detailed PFAS speciation, short-chain vs. long-chain performance, mass balances, energy use, and operational data (e.g., uptime, fouling, media replacement frequency) are not provided.

The reported 75% PFAS mass removal and <45% short-chain PFAS fraction are framed as treatment goals; the abstract does not clearly indicate whether these metrics were consistently achieved in operation.

The abstract does not address destruction or long-term chemical stability of PFAS on the Superloading adsorptive media returned to the landfill, so only phase transfer and concentration can be inferred.

comparability.reason: The source description establishes the treatment train (foam fractionation plus electrochemical oxidation) and general bench-scale conditions but does not provide quantitative removal, enrichment, or energy data that can be normalized or compared across studies.

endpoints.interpretation: Foam fractionation was used as a concentration step to transfer PFOA from bulk distilled water into a PFAS-enriched foamate fraction prior to electrochemical oxidation. The endpoint as described is phase transfer/enrichment rather than degradation.

Electrochemical oxidation with BDD electrodes was applied to the PFAS-enriched foamate to degrade PFOA; the study tracked fate using 14C labeling, but the snippet does not report quantitative removal or defluorination values.

limitations.statement: Experiments were conducted at bench scale in small (~200 mL) stirred batch reactors, which may limit direct extrapolation to pilot or full-scale systems.
